stories.headline: Expected fantasy points (xFP): 2026 leaderboard for WRs
stories.summary: xFP focuses solely on opportunity. Here are the leaders for 2026.
stories.body:
Expected fantasy points (xFP) strips away player talent and efficiency and focuses solely on opportunity.

FORP -- fantasy points over replacement player -- is the difference between a player's actual fantasy point total (FF points) and his xFP (or expected total).

Wide receiver adjustments are made as follows:

Rushing attempts: No change

Rushing yardage: Rush attempts multiplied by a rusher's expected yardage based on position and rush direction

Rushing touchdowns: Rushing xTD

Targets: No change

Receptions: Targets multiplied by a receiver's expected catch rate based on depth of throw, location and position

Receiving yardage: Targets multiplied by a receiver's expected yardage based on depth of throw, location and position

Receiving touchdowns: Receiving xTD

Two-point conversions: xTD multiplied by the league average 2-point rate

Fumbles lost: Touches multiplied by the league average rate

Return touchdowns: Excluded due to extreme rareness and randomness

stories.headline: Man City 'deserved' trophies - PSG boss Luis Enrique on charges
stories.summary: Paris Saint-Germain boss Luis Enrique has said Manchester City deserve to keep the trophies won during the period in which they have been found guilty of breaching Premier League rules.
stories.body:
Paris Saint-Germain boss Luis Enrique has said Manchester City deserve to keep the trophies won during the period in which they have been found guilty of breaching Premier League rules.

An independent commission found that City broke financial rules between 2009 and 2018. Sanctions have not yet been announced, but there have been calls for the club to be stripped of the three Premier League titles won during the nine-year period.

Luis Enrique, however, insists City -- who have appealed the judgement -- should keep their trophies.

"It's a surprise, but we need to respect the process and wait for the final decision," said Enrique.

"The authorities are responsible for making these decisions and we have to wait. If I speak only about football and the things I saw on the pitch, they deserved those trophies. We have to wait for the decision and nothing else."

Luis Enrique is preparing his Paris Saint-Germain team to play City in the Champions League on Wednesday.

Pep Guardiola is set to attend the game at the Etihad Stadium in a show of support for his former club. And Enrique insists the damning Premier League judgement should not taint what the former City boss achieved in Manchester.

- Regulator: English football must address finances 'before it is too late'

- Liverpool's Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai to miss Champions League clash with LASK

- Man City show defiance in wake of cheating scandal, trounce depleted Liverpool

"The trophies you win on the pitch remain on the pitch," said Enrique.

"They deserved to win that and I hope they can avoid the sanction. But we have to wait. The things I will say to Pep I will do in private.

"I hope everything works out well for Manchester City because what they've done on the pitch has been incredible."

stories.headline: WNBA Finals Games 3, 4 move to State Farm Arena to accommodate more fans
stories.summary: The WNBA announced Tuesday that Games 3 and 4 of the Finals between the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream will be played at State Farm Arena in Atlanta.
stories.body:
The Atlanta Dream will host Games 3 and 4 of the WNBA Finals at State Farm Arena, the home of the Atlanta Hawks, the franchise announced Tuesday morning. Game 3 has been moved from Oct. 22 to Oct. 21 while Game 4 will still be Oct. 24.

The WNBA Finals begin Saturday with the best-of-seven series between the Golden State Valkyries and the Dream, with Golden State hosting the first two games. The location of the Dream home games had been undecided as the team wanted to play in a bigger space than the Gateway Center Arena at College Park, which has been its home arena since 2021 and holds just 3,500 fans.

Six of the Dream's regular-season games this season, and all three playoff games, have been played at State Farm, which seats more than 17,000 fans. The arena was booked for a Sombr concert on Oct. 22 and Hawks regular-season games Oct. 24 and 29. Game 3 was moved a day earlier, and the Hawks changed their tipoff against the Houston Rockets from 8 p.m. to 8:30 on Oct. 24. The Valkyries and Dream will tip at 1 p.m. instead of 3:30.

"The change of venue dramatically expands the seating capacity," WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert said in a statement, "and ensures that the Dream will be able to provide an extraordinary atmosphere for the first WNBA Finals game to be played in the Atlanta market since 2013. We are pleased that thousands more fans across the Southeast region will have the opportunity to experience the ultimate WNBA action -- the WNBA Finals -- in person."

Dream majority owner Larry Gottesdiener added, "This is what the players and the fans deserve. We are grateful to all of the stakeholders who worked together to resolve the conflicts and make this happen."

The Valkyries, who will host Games 1, 2, and also 5 and 7 (if necessary), had their own conflict with Game 2 on Oct. 19. A Doja Cat concert was scheduled that night at Chase Center (capacity 18,064) in San Francisco. The concert was moved to Oct. 25.

stories.headline: Hurricanes captain Jordan Staal to miss 1-2 months with torn calf muscle
stories.summary: Hurricanes captain Jordan Staal, the playoff MVP in their Stanley Cup championship run last season, will miss one to two months with a torn calf muscle.
stories.body:
Carolina Hurricanes captain Jordan Staal, the playoff MVP in their Stanley Cup championship run last season, will miss one to two months with a torn calf muscle, the team announced Tuesday.

Staal, 38, was a late scratch for the Hurricanes' game in Philadelphia on Sunday. He suffered the injury while warming up before Carolina's pregame skate.

Coach Rod Brind'Amour said after the game that the injury "came up last minute" and that "hopefully, it's nothing serious" that would keep Staal out long term. On Tuesday, Brind'Amour offered an update, saying Staal's partially torn calf muscle will keep him out "anywhere from a month to two months."

Staal had no points in six games for Carolina, which is 5-1-1 to start the season. Playing in his 21st season, Staal is considered one of the best defensive forwards in the NHL, anchoring an effective third line with wingers Jordan Martinook and Nikolaj Ehlers.

Staal was a driving force behind Carolina's Stanley Cup Final win over the Vegas Golden Knights, scoring six goals in six games. Overall, he had 12 points in 19 postseason games while shutting down top offensive opponents, earning the Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff MVP.

The center, who has also played for the Pittsburgh Penguins, has 1,409 career games, 318 goals and 429 assists (747 points). He's a two-time finalist for the Selke Trophy as the NHL's best defensive forward but has yet to win the award.

The Hurricanes host the Washington Capitals as part of the NHL Frozen Frenzy on Tuesday night.

stories.headline: Who is this year's Mr. October? Tracking the playoff MVP for 2026
stories.summary: We go inside the numbers on the players doing the most to help their teams win.
stories.body:
Who is hero of the 2026 MLB playoffs?

To try to answer to that question, we're tabulating the cumulative win probability added figures for every player in the postseason. But we've added a twist: The deeper we get into the playoffs, the more weight the WPA carries. The division series counts double the wild-card round, then we'll double it again for the championship series and, finally, once again for the World Series.

This means that players who shine in the early rounds can still get on the leaderboard, but it's more difficult. Coming through when the championship leverage is at its highest is what becoming an October hero is all about.

Monday's hero: A year ago, Chase DeLauter had just made his big-league debut in the postseason for Cleveland, though his after-the-season promotion couldn't get the Guardians back to the ALCS. Cleveland is there this time, and DeLauter was a central part of the Guardians' late-inning explosion against Drew Rasmussen and the Rays' bullpen in Game 1. DeLauter had three hits, one a homer off Rasmussen to get Cleveland on the board, then stroked a go-ahead double in the eighth. Led by Jose Ramirez, the Guardians suddenly-hot offense now lands three hitters in the top 10 of the Hero standings.

Methodology
As mentioned above, each player's win probability added (WPA) is tracked on a per-game basis. Each round of the playoffs counts double that of the previous round. The tabulation is then converted to an AXE-style index in which 100 represents the average for all postseason players. The "Change" column looks in the changes in AXE numbers from the previous day for players who were in action. You can sort this column by clicking on it to see the day's heroes.

stories.headline: Christian Horner: Mercedes' Toto Wolff has it 'easy' at the moment
stories.summary: Former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner has suggested that Mercedes boss Toto Wolff has "got it quite easy" at the moment.
stories.body:
Former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner has suggested that Mercedes boss Toto Wolff has "got it quite easy" at the moment.

Horner, 52, officially left Red Bull Racing in September last year having been relieved of "operational duties" following last July's British Grand Prix. It ended a 20-year career with the team, where he won eight drivers' and six constructors' titles.

The past decade saw Horner spar with Wolff as Red Bull and Mercedes did battle.

This season, Horner's old team are currently fourth in the constructors' standings with 11 podiums and two wins, both claimed by Max Verstappen during this month's races in Bahrain and Singapore.

Mercedes top the constructors' leaderboard, while Kimi Antonelli is first in the drivers' standings having won eight races so far.

A potential return to F1 for Horner remains a hot topic and in an interview earlier this year, Wolff suggested Horner had "broken a lot of glass."

In an interview with the Guardian, Horner said: "He [Wolff] also said this [Red Bull] engine was going to be completely s--t and a disaster.

"Toto's got it quite easy at the moment. Zak Brown [head of McLaren] is compromised because he's using Toto's engine so he can't ruffle feathers.

"All sport needs rivalry, whether it's [Alex] Ferguson and [Arsene] Wenger, [Jose] Mourinho and (Pep) Guardiola. It percolates and polarises. I used that to galvanise good people to take on Mercedes."

- Formula 1 to return to Africa in 'early 2030s' as Rwanda race confirmed

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Toto Wolff finds quirky solution to Kimi Antonelli track limits 'stress'

Horner also revealed in the interview that he has suffered from panic attacks and has worked to recognise the symptoms.

"I didn't know what it was. You suddenly feel dizzy and conscious of your breathing and you think there's something strange going on. I put it down to having had too much coffee on an oppressive, muggy, thundery day," he said.

"Then it happened again. I got checked out and there was nothing physically the matter. They said: 'We think you have anxiety. Your breathing's very shallow.' It was my body telling me you're pushing pretty hard here. I'm able to recognise the symptoms now and let it go, and breathe."

stories.headline: AFL player movement tracker: trade requests, free agency latest, who's on the move?
stories.summary: The offseason is upon us which means AFL trades, free agency, and player movement is about to take off. Here's the latest news, whispers, and confirmed deals.
stories.body:
It's AFL player movement season, with trades and free agency set to dominate the month of October. So who is going where? Keep track with our player movement guide here.

When is the AFL trade and free agency window?
The 2026 AFL trade period commences on Monday, October 5 and closes in the evening of Wednesday, October 14.

The free agency window opens and closes a little earlier; it runs from Friday, October 2 until Friday, October 9.

Tuesday, Oct. 13
Blues land gun Giant

Lachie Whitfield's move to Carlton is official, with the 32-year-old joining the Blues on a three-year deal. Whitfield has played 278 games, and joins Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, and Jake Stringer in departing the Giants.

Carlton receive picks 31 and 50 along with the veteran, with pick 25, pick 26, and a 2028 third-round pick going back the other way.

Former top-five pick on the move

Zane Duursma has got his wish, joining Melbourne along with pick 52. The Roos get pick 33 and 49 in return.

Blues ruck crosses to Collingwood

Flynn Riley has been traded to the Magpies after joining Carlton in the mid-season draft this year, making his AFL debut in Round 18.

A 2028 third-round pick goes the Blues' way.

Swans trade star defender to North Melbourne

The biggest name left on the AFL trade board has tumbled, with Sydney agreeing to move Nick Blakey to North Melbourne.

The Swans offloaded Blakey, draft pick No.52 and their 2028 second-round selection in exchange for a glut of picks.

The Kangaroos traded picks No.6 and No.47, a 2027 second-round pick, a 2028 first-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to get the deal done.

Monday Oct. 12
Suns land Schubert, Butler from Hawks

The Suns have landed their offseason trade target in Aidan Schubert from Hawthorn, in a package also involving Sam Butler and some picks going both ways.

Gold Coast gained Schubert, Butler, Hawthorn's 2028 first-round pick, and Hawthorn's 2027 third-round pick, in exchange for Gold Coast's 2028 first-rounder, and second rounders in both 2027 and 2028.

Friday, Oct. 9
Butters is a Bulldog

Zak Butters is officially a Western Bulldog. Port Adelaide will not match the offer and accept pick No. 5 as compensation, having also earlier secured picks 6, 10, and two future-firsts in the five-club mega trade. The star free agent and three-time All-Australian, who played 156 games and kicked 73 goals for the Power after being drafted in 2019, has signed a nine-year deal with his boyhood club

Hawks land spearhead King

After securing Zach Merrett earlier this week, Hawthorn have officially welcomed Ben King today after gold Coast elected not to match the offer for the restricted free agent. the Suns will receive a first round pick as compensation, which currently stands at pick No. 7.

Mega trade approved

The league approved a mega trade involving Port Adelaide, the Bulldogs, Melbourne, Hawthorn and Carlton, two players and scores of picks.

Under the five-team deal, the Bulldogs gave up picks No. 12 and No. 31 and a 2028 first-rounder to bring in Hawthorn's Finn Maginness, Carlton's Hudson O'Keeffe and later picks in this year's draft and future years.

Port parted with picks No. 4, 46 and 81 and six second-round or worse future selections to get back picks No. 6 and No. 10, Melbourne's 2027 first-rounder and the Dogs' 2028 first-rounder.

The Demons surrendered picks No.6, 10 and 87 and their 2027 first-rounder -- as well as two late future picks -- for picks No. 4, 12, 31 and 46.

Hawthorn (2027 third-rounder) and Carlton (2028 fourth-rounder) received late future picks for Maginness and O'Keeffe.

-- AAP

Flag Lion gets his wish

Brisbane has traded second-year Lion and 2025 premiership player Sam Marshall and pick No. 39 to St Kilda for a 2027 first-rounder.

Thursday, Oct. 8
Marshall lands at the Cats

St Kilda have pulled the trigger on a deal to send contracted ruckman Rowan Marshall to Geelong, as the Cats and other rival clubs circle Sydney star Nick Blakey.

Geelong traded pick No.14 in this year's draft for the disenchanted 30-year-old and a third-round selection in 2028 on Thursday afternoon.

New Zealand-born Marshall had requested a move to the Cats for a second straight year after St Kilda recruited Tom De Koning to become their first-choice ruckman.

-- AAP

Wednesday, Oct. 7
Dons defender gets traded to the Cats

After being denied a trade last year, Jordan Ridley got his wish for a fresh start after Essendon and Geelong agreed to a deal on Wednesday.

Geelong gave up utility Jack Bowes, a 2027 first-round pick and 2028 second-round pick to get the 27-year-old Ridley through the door.

Pick No. 60 and a 2028 fourth-round selection will come back to the Cats from the Bombers.

--AAP

Tuesday, Oct. 6
O'Driscoll makes the move over east

Fremantle have traded 24-year-old Nathan O'Driscoll to Richmond in exchange for pick 61 in this year's draft.

The winger played 17 games for the Dockers this season but wasn't selected for the Grand Final.

Monday, Oct. 5
TRADE PERIOD OPENS
Merrett finally becomes a Hawk

After attempting to join Hawthorn last year, Zach Merrett has finally been traded from Essendon to the Hawks.

Hawthorn have sent picks 15, 25 and a 2028 second-round pick in exchange for the 31-year-old.

Merrett leaves the Bombers a week after winning a record-equaling seventh Crichton Medal, three All-Australian blazers, and 274 games.

Pendlebury becomes a Sun

AFL games record holder Scott Pendlebury is officially a Sun after Gold Coast and Collingwood agreed on a trade for the 38-year-old veteran.

Pendlebury, a two-time premiership player, heads to the Suns in exchange for pick No. 65 in this year's draft.

"It's an exciting group here at the SUNS and the opportunity to bring a few different ideas and also learn from a great group of coaches and players is one I'm really looking forward to," Pendlebury told the Suns.

"This side is one I've watched from afar and really admired. I've got a bit of knowledge about the industry so I'm here to play my role and help this squad continue to develop."

Jesse Hogan traded from GWS to Collingwood

Out-of-favour Giants forward Jesse Hogan has made the switch to Collingwood in exchange for pick 75.

The 31-year-old won the Coleman Medal in 2024 but has been unable to recapture his best form at the Giants in the two years since.

Magpies list boss Justin Leppitsch said Hogan would be a valuable addition.

"On behalf of everyone at Collingwood, I'd like to warmly welcome Jesse to Collingwood. Jesse has established himself as one of the competition's premier key forwards and we're excited to see him bring his experience and talent to our club," he said.

"His aerial presence inside forward-50 and his consistency as a goal-kicker make him a genuine threat.

"Like Lachie (Neale), Jesse has a passion to teach the next generation and will make a great addition to our club."

Saturday, Oct. 3
Bulldogs seal free-agency signing of key defender

The Western Bulldogs have finally snagged the key defender they need, securing Adelaide backman Jordon Butts as an unrestricted free agent.

The Bulldogs are set for a bumper AFL trade period headlined by working through a deal for Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters, ahead of a 2027 season where the club will have high expectations.

But after seeing off Carlton's advances to keep hold of defender Buku Khamis, the Bulldogs have filled a major area of need by adding 26-year-old Butts.

Adelaide will receive a second-round compensation selection, currently pick No.33, in this year's draft.

-- AAP

Friday, Oct. 2
FREE AGENCY OPEN
Three-peat Lion locks in Magpies move

Lachie Neale has sealed his high-profile switch to Collingwood, with Brisbane teasing the dual Brownlow medallist on his way out the door.

The AFL approved Neale signing a three-year deal with the Magpies on Friday afternoon, closing out the first day of free agency.

The 33-year-old ball-winner leaves as an unrestricted free agent after the Lions clinched a third straight flag with their stunning seven-point grand final victory over Fremantle.

-- AAP

Greene on his way to the Cats

Toby Greene will join Geelong as an unrestricted free agent on a three-year deal, re-partnering with former Giants teammate Jeremey Cameron.

The paperwork was lodged to the AFL on Friday morning.

The Giants receive band three compensation for Greene, which is currently pick No. 26 in the upcoming draft.

Greene departs the Giants with his name etched in the club's record books, sitting first in games played for the club with a tally of 282 games, as well as leading the club's all-time goalkicking tally with 450 majors.

Briggs now a Tiger

Richmond has landed GWS ruck Kieren Briggs as an unrestricted free agent.

Briggs' move to the Tigers was confirmed just hours after the free agency window opened on Friday.

Briggs played 88 games for GWS after joining the club as the No.34 pick in the 2018 draft.

Amartey officially joins the Blues

Free agency has opened with a bang, with out-of-favour key forward Joel Amartey committing to Carlton.

Details are still to come on the length of contract, and Sydney's compensation.

Hawthorn father-son recommits despite interest

Calsher Dear has made a shock decision to re-sign with the Hawks for two years, despite being out of favour thorughout 2026.

The 20-year-old has kicked 39 goals from 31 games, but found himself behind Jack Gunston, Mitch Lewis and Mabior Chol. With Gunston signed on and Suns forward Ben King expected to sign with the Hawks as well, there were questions about whether Dear would get enough opportunity at his childhood club.

Hawks list boss Mark McKenzie said the club was "really pleased" that Dear had recommitted.

"He remains an important part of what we are trying to achieve as a club," he said.

"Following his debut season, Calsher showed us all the special talent that he is, but as a key tall at 21 years of age, we've needed to be patient with his progression.

"Having battled several injuries over his first three seasons in the system, we are very excited about what the future holds for Calsher with a strong pre-season under his belt and greater continuity into 2027 and beyond."

Thursday, Oct. 1
Goater set to make cross-city switch

North Melbourne defender Josh Goater is set to join the Hawks after requesting a trade on Thursday.

Having played just 18 games, the 23-year-old had fallen out of favour after an injury-hit run in his time at North.

Premiership Lion requests trade

The Brisbane Lions have confirmed Sam Marshall has requested a trade to St Kilda.

"The Brisbane Lions confirm premiership midfielder Sam Marshall has requested to be traded to St Kilda," the Lions said in a statement.

"Marshall has played 13 games, including the 2025 Premiership, across two seasons since being selected in the first round of the 2024 draft as a graduate of the Youi Brisbane Lions Academy.

"The club respects Marshall's request to be traded, and will work towards facilitating an outcome that best reflects true value to the Brisbane Lions for the 20-year-old."

Tuesday, Sept. 29
Neale informs Lions he intends to join Collingwood

Two-time Brownlow Medal winner Lachie Neale has told Brisbane he will depart the club as an unrestricted free agent and sign a three-year deal with Collingwood.

Aware that Neale intended to leave at the end of the year, the Lions never offered him a new contract.

The paperwork for the deal is expected to be formalised as early as Friday when the free agency period opens.

Friday, Sept. 25
Jordon Butts to join the Bulldogs

Zak Butters isn't the only South Australian-based player keen to join the Western Bulldogs, with Crows' key defender Jordon Butts officially naming the Dogs as his preferred offseason destination.

The unrestricted free agent will sign a five-year deal at the Kennel, according to AFL.com.au.

Tuesday, Sept. 22
Amartey officially names Carlton

Wantaway Sydney forward Joel Amartey has confirmed his desire to join Carlton as an unrestricted free agent.

The 26-year-old was kept out of the Swans' side with an Achilles injury in the latter stages of the year.

With Charlie Curnow (75 goals in 2026) and Logan McDonald (51) cementing their spots in the Sydney forward line as the prime targets, Amartey is hoping for more opportunity at the Blues.

Thursday, Sept. 17
GWS captain finally makes big call on his future

Toby Greene has opted to leave GWS, telling the AFL club he wishes to play with Geelong next season. Greene, who has been at the Giants since their foundation season in 2012, wants to go back to Victoria for family reasons.

In an extraordinary way to announce the decision, outgoing GWS boss Dave Matthews confirmed Greene's intentions on radio, before the club released a statement.

The 32-year-old has been offered a lucrative three-year deal to join the Cats.

Saturday, Sept. 12
Zak Butters makes huge free agency call
The year's hottest restricted free agent Zak Butters has made a huge call on his future, nominating the Western Bulldogs as his preferred destination.

After a year of speculation, with Geelong thought to be the front-runner for the Power star's signature, Butters made the call on Saturday, first reported by AFL.com.au's Callum Twomey.

The deal is reportedly for nine years.

Thursday, Sept. 10
Hogan set to join Pies
GWS and Collingwood have both confirmed that 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan has chosen the Magpies at his next home.

Set to be a four-club player, Hogan is 31 and coming off a 12-goal season from just nine appearances.

It's a big boost for the Magpies if Hogan can recapture his form; key forward has been an area of concern for a number of years.

Tuesday, Sept. 8
Bailey set to be Lion for life
Brisbane's Zac Bailey has ended months of 'will he, won't he' speculation to sign with the Lions for eight years, taking him through the 2034 season, the the club confirmed on Tuesday.

Bailey, a free agent, had been a big target for the Crows, who had reportedly tabled a more lucrative offer.

"I'm absolutely rapt to be staying at the Brisbane Lions," Bailey said in a statement.

"I love the environment here, the players, coaches and staff who all make it a great place to be and I feel like this Club continues to bring the best out of me.

"This Club means so much to me - I came here as a young player and have grown up here and to know I will be here long-term is something I'm really proud of.

"I would like to thank the club, my partner Em, my family and my management for being so supportive throughout this process.

"I love what we as a club have achieved during my time here and I am super excited about what we can continue to achieve together."

Rowan Marshall requests trade
St Kilda ruck Rowan Marshall looks set to be on the move, with the Saints confirming the big man had requested a trade for the second straight season.

While Marshall hasn't requested a specific club, it's likely to be Geelong after he failed to secure a trade to the Cats last year. He played 21 games for the Saints this seaosn, juggling ruck duties with Tom De Koning, who came in from Carlton last offseason.

"Rowan is a highly valued member of the St Kilda Football Club and remains contracted until the end of 2027," the Saints said in a statement.

"Marshall has not nominated a preferred destination at this stage, with the club making clear that any trade will need to be in the best interests of the St Kilda Football Club."

Zane Duursma wants to go to Melbourne
The No. 4 pick in the 2023 AFL draft Zane Duursma has requested a trade out of North Melbourne, with Melbourne in his sights.

The news comes a week after coach Alastair Clarkson was sacked by the club. North won nine games in 2026, their best return since 2019.

Ed Allan re-signs with the Pies
After speculation about his future at the Magpies, mdifielder Ed Allan has put pen to paper, signing a four year extension to remain at Collingwood.

2026 was a breakout season for Allan, who played 19 games and averaged a career-high 16.5 disposals per game.

Monday, Sept. 7

stories.headline: NRL: Spencer Leniu signs with Eels after early Roosters release
stories.summary: Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.
stories.body:
Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

Leniu finished his three-year stint at the Tricolours on a high after a stellar performance in their 19-18 win over Newcastle to secure the 2026 trophy.

The NSW Origin representative added the Roosters' premiership ring to the three he won with Penrith from 2021-2023.

Leniu was granted a release from the final year of his Roosters contract, which will give the club some salary cap reprieve

The hard-hitting forward's Eels contract is reportedly worth more than the $850,000 per year he was making with Easts, where he spent much of his time coming off the bench.

He is expected to play a more active role in blue and gold, leading the line for the Eels' forward pack.

The westward move will see the former Panther reunite with good friend Jarome Luai, but first the pair will both suit up for Toa Samoa at the Rugby League World Cup.

Eels general manager of football Mark O'Neill shared his delight at signing one of the game's "premier enforcers".

"We're thrilled to have Spencer join the Parramatta Eels and become part of what we're building at this club," O'Neill said in a statement.

"He's one of the elite middle forwards in the game and has consistently performed on the biggest stages throughout his career.

The exit of Leniu adds to the exodus of stars from the Roosters premiership lineup.

Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase are rugby-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans is joining Hull FC, while Daniel Tupou retired this week after his 307-game career.

Connor Watson, who missed the title decider due to concussion, has signed for a season with St George Illawarra Dragons.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson said Leniu had been a strong contributor during his time at the club.

"Spencer has brought a lot to our group over the last three years, both through the way he plays and the energy and personality he brings every day," Robinson said in a statement on Thursday.

"He brings an intensity and competitiveness to everything he does, and he challenges the people around him to be better.

"To see him finish his time here as a premiership winner is something he should be really proud of, and something we'll always share together."

With his departure announced at the Roosters' awards night on Wednesday, Leniu said he would leave the club on a high.

""I'm proud to have worn the Roosters jersey and I'll always have a lot of love and respect for the club, the boys and everyone who has supported me during my time here," said Leniu.

"Winning a premiership with this group and sharing that with the boys, our families and everyone at the club is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life."

stories.body:
Expected fantasy points (xFP) strip away player talent and efficiency and focus solely on opportunity.

FORP -- fantasy points over replacement player -- is the difference between a player's actual fantasy point total (FF points) and his xFP (expected total).

Running back adjustments are made as follows:

Rushing attempts: No change

Rushing yardage: Rush attempts multiplied by a rusher's expected yardage based on position, in-box defenders and rush direction

Rushing touchdowns: Rushing xTD

Targets: No change

Receptions: Targets multiplied by a receiver's expected catch rate based on depth of throw, location and position

Receiving yardage: Targets multiplied by a receiver's expected yardage based on depth of throw, location and position

Receiving touchdowns: Receiving xTD

Two-point conversions: xTD multiplied by the league average two-point rate

Fumbles lost: Touches multiplied by the league average rate

stories.headline: Regulator: English football must address finances 'before it is too late'
stories.summary: The chair of the Independent Football Regulator says the English game must "act before it is too late" to tackle the financial dangers facing it.
stories.body:
The chair of the Independent Football Regulator says the English game must "act before it is too late" to tackle the financial dangers facing it.

The IFR published its draft 'State of the Game' report on Tuesday which found that while English football generated £9 billion ($11.9bn) in revenue last season, 94% of clubs in the top five divisions were loss-making.

Thirty-two clubs could not survive more than 30 days without owner funding, the report found, while 17 would be loss-making even if their players played for free.

IFR chair David Kogan said in the report's foreword that English club football was simultaneously the "richest, best and most deeply competitive in the world while also standing on the edge of financial disaster."

- Football Regulator chair will quit if politics interferes with any Man City investigation

The report forecasts total debt in English football would rise above £5bn ($6.6bn) by the end of this season, and that net transfer debt was approximately £3.4bn ($4.5bn), at a time when broadcast revenues are predicted to plateau or decline in the next cycle.

Kogan told the Press Association: "Everyone needs to take into account the fact that nothing is ever forever.

"We have to look at [the potential for broadcast revenues to fall] as a risk factor, and just make a judgement call, and actually also see what happens if the money does reduce.

"At the moment, the sun is shining. There's £9bn a year coming in. This is the very moment to address the issues of liquidity and losses and debt, before suddenly you see the money going backwards and it's too late.

"And our intention is to act before it's too late. And I believe, actually, the world of football wants that, and that's what we're going to do."

The IFR's action plan calls for reform to football's distribution mechanisms, finding that the average Premier League club earned 8.7 times more than the average Championship club in the 2024-25 season, compared to 2.7 times in 1992-93, the first season of the Premier League.

Kogan has been in the room with the Premier League and the EFL in recent months as they continue discussions over a 'New Deal' on funding and cost controls between the leagues.

"I have observed them dealing with issue after issue after issue, and reaching broad consensus on those issues, and inherently believe that the deal they're talking about now, if it comes off, might be effective in addressing some of the issues that we raise," he said.

One sticking point has always been parachute payments to clubs relegated from the Premier League. The report finds these are "distortive" and encourage overspending by Championship clubs, but also highlighted why they are necessary, finding that the clubs relegated from the top flight in 2024-25 saw a £70 million ($92.5m) average drop in revenue.

Kogan pointed out that the deal under discussion includes merit rakes, whereby a proportion of the solidarity funding from the Premier League to the EFL will be paid based on league position.

"Clubs in the top 10 positions of the Championship are going to receive more money," Kogan said.

"Clubs being relegated [who are] due parachute payments are going to get less money and the delta, which was 'that' [hands wide apart], is going to go to 'that' [hands closer together].

"Does that achieve everything that the EFL might have wanted three or four years ago? No. But it goes a long way towards addressing the issue. There are a lot of moving parts here and we hope they reach an agreement."

To tackle clubs' reliance on owner funding, clubs will be required as part of the IFR's licensing system to commit to an action plan setting out how they will meet the 'Appropriate Financial Resources' requirement by 2030.

- Enzo Maresca on Man City celebration at Anfield: 'What do you want us to do?'

- Steven Gerrard says Man City must be stripped of titles after guilty verdict: 'Make them suffer'

- Why did Man City fans bring inflatable bananas to Anfield?

Also, IFR chief executive Richard Monks said the regulator's team was alive as part of its licensing regime to what the report describes as "creative compliance" with existing competition rules, such as Chelsea selling hotels to companies linked to their ownership in order to meet Premier League financial rules.

"They understand what's going on, and crucially, they're a cynical bunch," he said.

"However a rule is phrased, a regulator should look at that rule and think, 'What do we think a club would do in that situation with that rule?' They will legitimately try and push the boundaries as far as they possibly can.

"[That is] perfectly reasonable. Your job as an effective regulator is to anticipate that, and therefore both write the rules but also supervise in a way that you manage those issues."

Football Supporters' Association chair Tom Greatrex called on the authorities to act on the IFR's findings and said that the report must be an "alarm call" which leads to "real and lasting change."

State of the Game report - action plan

The six-point action plan proposed by the report to improve English football's financial sustainability is as follows:

The distribution of revenue must be reformed, with changes focused on financial stability and not encourage imprudent spending. This reform should seek to "mitigate the financial impact of relegation from the Premier League" and "reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship."
Leagues, clubs and other stakeholders should take actions to reduce losses.
Action should be taken at the National League level to ensure football governance matches the risk within the game.
Clubs must improve how they manage financial risk. By 2030, the Football Governance Act requires clubs to hold 'Appropriate Financial Resources.' The IFR will require all clubs to commit to an action plan setting out how they will meet the 'Appropriate Financial Resources' requirement by 2030.
Clubs must show how they take fans' views into account.
Clubs must make progress on boardroom and senior executive diversity.

The IFR has also undertaken to produce an annual risk assessment, with the first to be published in the spring of 2028.

stories.headline: Tyrese Haliburton's return brings hope and expectations in Indiana
stories.summary: Nearly 16 months ago, a torn Achilles cost Tyrese Haliburton -- and the Pacers -- the 2025-26 season. Now, he returns to help them reclaim their spot in the East.
stories.body:
THE SWEAT FROM Tyrese Haliburton's Indiana Pacers jersey almost immediately began to seep into his blue warmup shirt.

For 16 months, the two-time All-Star guard had been patiently -- and then not so patiently -- and then practically champing at the bit to leave his seat on the sideline and play minutes in an NBA game.

On Oct. 7, he finally did. The Pacers were playing in Ames, Iowa, at Iowa State University, Haliburton's alma mater, where it was a two-part homecoming.

It was his first game at his college arena in six years. Students began lining up the night before the game to get into the student section and grab a yellow shirt with Haliburton's face on it over the moniker "Cyclone Hali." And it was also Haliburton's first seven minutes in a game since tearing his right Achilles during Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals.

With 4:27 remaining in the first quarter of the Pacers' preseason opener against the Minnesota Timberwolves on Oct. 7, Haliburton relished a different moment: his first break.

"I was tired as hell," Haliburton said with a laugh after the game. "But even through that, I just kept feeling like, 'Man, I'm playing again.'"

On Indiana's first possession of the game, an antsy Haliburton fired a no-look pass, intended for Andrew Nembhard, out of bounds. But with that out of the way, on the next possession, Haliburton ran a 2-on-1 with Pascal Siakam that Haliburton finished with a crossover into a 15-foot jumper for his first basket in more than a year.

The adrenaline of the night carried him through 16 minutes of action. Haliburton finished with seven points and six assists in the Pacers' 123-112 win.

"I have my own internal expectations," Haliburton told ESPN. "But our goal is to win a championship. That has never wavered."

The Pacers' season -- and Indiana's road back to contention -- depends on those expectations.

The last time Haliburton was healthy, he electrified the NBA with one of the greatest clutch postseason runs in NBA history, with a game-tying or winning shot in each of the four rounds of the 2025 playoffs.

Indiana led in the first quarter of Game 7 in Oklahoma City before Haliburton tore his Achilles, and the Thunder marched their way to the record books.

While Haliburton spent the 2025-26 season recovering, the Pacers won 19 games.

It makes Indiana one of the most perplexing teams coming into the 2026-27 NBA season. Despite making the conference finals in 2024 and the conference finals in 2025, the Pacers are projected to win a modest 42 games and ranked 10th in the Eastern Conference, according to ESPN's Basketball Power Index.

"I don't look too much into it," Haliburton told ESPN. "Our whole team can relate to that. We've all felt that way one way or another."

The Pacers are the last team to beat the champion New York Knicks in a playoff series. But in a more competitive East than the last one he left, Haliburton is out to prove that the Pacers can reclaim their spot at the top.

"Finding that magic again, that's no guarantee," Pacers general manager Chad Buchanan told ESPN. "But our core guys believe in each other. They feel like people have written them off already. That's what's happened those two years we made runs -- people just kind of discarded us. That's what fuels them."

THE ZERO IN the middle of the jersey was orange, matching the trim on a jersey that had been shaded with blue in the middle. As Haliburton picked up the sheet of paper, he scoffed.

"Who drew this one?" he asked. "Orange and blue on a Pacers jersey?"

"Knicks colors," his wife, Jade, said with a knowing smile.

With training camp still a few weeks away, the Haliburtons visited children at the Peyton Manning Children's Hospital in Indianapolis.

Haliburton was there as a spokesperson for the Indiana Donor Network to raise awareness for organ donation. The five kids in attendance are recipients of kidney transplants.

Sitting around a table, Haliburton and the children, some as young as 6, gathered sheets of paper to color. A raucous debate immediately ensued.

"What's your favorite color?" Haliburton asked his tablemates, launching an animated discussion.

"Red!" one kid said. "Blue!" said another. "Yellow!"

"Rainbow!" another said, inciting another debate as to whether all the colors can be considered one color. He insisted it could.

"But is there a rainbow marker?" Haliburton prods, presenting the question as a color-form of checkmate. When Haliburton suggests his favorite color is grey, the kids recoil. "You never hear that, huh?" he says with a smile.

Haliburton spent much of the past year in Indianapolis launching himself into projects such as these.

He helped the Pacers revitalize their charity softball game earlier this summer, featuring players from the Indianapolis Colts and Indiana Fever. Fans packed Victory Field, a 12,000-seat Triple-A baseball stadium in downtown Indianapolis.

Haliburton's connection to the Midwest is deep. He was born in Wisconsin and met and eventually proposed to his wife in Ames. His bond to the region has only deepened since he was traded to Indiana in 2022.

It's why he has poured so much into the community.

"It's a different perspective on life now," Haliburton told ESPN. "I'm just thankful to be playing basketball again and to be doing all the different things that I can do in the community because when something like that happens, it's like your life flashes before your eyes."

During his first vacation a few months after surgery, he could barely walk down the stairs at a house they had rented and needed assistance getting around when they left. His surgeon had warned him, but the reality had set in. He wept in the shower.

"Just having to come to terms with going from being on top of the world to the complete opposite of that in an instance," Haliburton told ESPN.

"It's such a crazy thing to say because it's a basketball injury that no matter what ... there's a time put on it. You know you're going to be good in that amount of time. We have the best doctors in the world, the best therapists, all those things. You know you're going to be good, but it's a scary thing."

He spent most of his recovery in Indianapolis, finding a spot on the bench for game nights, home and road, even as the season went south. But in the middle of his rehab, he dealt with a bad case of the shingles, too, gaining 30 pounds and suffering from severe face swelling as a side effect of the heavy medication. The illness, which is highly contagious, kept him away from his teammates on the sidelines. It was another blow in a long season.

"In the league, especially when a star player like that is injured, what that means for the next year, sometimes they're on their own little schedule, 'Hey, I just got to do what's right for me,'" Buchanan said. "That's not how Ty's wired. Ty is wired to know what does the team need from me, rather than what I need to do for the team."

During his lonely, arduous recovery, he would occasionally fire up some of his old highlights.

"Just to feel something," he said. "I once could do that. I miss that feeling."

At one point, he even rewatched the 2025 Finals, he said. His focus remained on Game 4. The Pacers were leading 2-1, but the Thunder rallied from down double-digits in the second half as Shai Gilgeous-Alexander scored 15 of his 35 points in the final 4:38 of the game.

"Game 4 will forever live in my brain," Haliburton said. "You win that game, the whole series changes."

The thought sat with him as he watched his team go through its worst season in franchise history, realizing so much of the conversation around the Pacers' struggles centered on him, his injury, his recovery and his eventual return.

"Everybody always feels the summer is really long," Haliburton said. "Well, I've had that for double, triple the amount of time everybody else."

HALIBURTON DOESN'T WANT the Pacers to forget last season.

Indiana finished with its fewest wins in franchise history. The team was decimated by injuries early, and started to position itself for a better draft pick by the second half. By the end of the season, the team looked like a shell of the one that went to the Finals.

"You can take [our preseason rankings] as disrespect, but at the same time, you got to understand we put ourselves in that position by the way we played last year," Haliburton said. "There's standards that we didn't meet that we got to get back to. And there's no secret that there was a drop-off last year."

Training camp has been focused on rebuilding those habits.

The night before the first day of practice, the team gathered at Buchanan's house on the floor at his indoor basketball court. It has become an annual tradition for the past four years, a moment when the Pacers can iron out their priorities heading into the season.

Coach Rick Carlisle lamented how long the summer had been. It had been 5½ months since their last game in April, and even longer since their last game with anything on the line.

"Reclaim" ended up being the key word during the meeting.

Carlisle acknowledged how important it was to have Haliburton back, but cautioned against looking at Haliburton as a savior.

"We're a team that's very reliant on one another," Carlisle said before the game in Ames last week. "One of the things that when we had a really, really good two-year run, it made us a special team, our connectivity, our ecosystem, dependence on one another.

"We're always going to be better as the sum of all the parts."

Most of the Pacers' core is the same -- Haliburton, Siakam, Nembhard and Aaron Nesmith -- but Ivica Zubac was brought in to replace the departed Myles Turner in a trade deadline deal that ended up costing Indiana the No. 5 pick in the draft.

Team sources say the Pacers are confident that the deal will help reopen their championship window. They also acknowledge Zubac, who plays closer to the basket, will provide different strengths than Turner, a center who stretches the floor from 3-point range.

"We have a great coach who figures things out," Buchanan told ESPN. "That's a strength of his. If things aren't going well, and we aren't playing well -- or [Zubac's] not fitting well, he adapts."

The fit with Zubac could take time. His individual fit with Haliburton could, too. They've struggled with their timing in pick-and-rolls early in the preseason, with Haliburton often rounding the corner before his new center has an opportunity to roll.

"He's so anxious to prove to people. He hates that people say he'll have to be patient. He hates that," Buchanan told ESPN. "He's like, 'I've been out 16 effing months. I'm ready to play.' He's obviously very confident, but I still think there's going to be a ramp-up for him as just getting his feet, groove and rhythm back."

HALIBURTON MOVED LIKE his former self at times, but the growing pains were evident in his first game back.

He compared himself to a rookie, playing too fast and needing to slow down to let the offense find its rhythm. He tweaked his right ankle during the game, and sat out the next preseason game, but an MRI confirmed his Achilles was unaffected.

"I was hyped to be out there, excited, but I just got to slow down a little bit," he said. "There's a ton of improvement to be made on my end and on our team's end. But I'm just excited to be back on the floor."

Multiple moments in the gym this summer gave him reason for the confidence.

One afternoon in late July, 13 months after his surgery, he took one dribble and tossed the ball into the air toward the basket. As he raced after it, the ball bounced just short of the basket inside the Pacers' practice facility, its upward trajectory almost carrying him higher toward the rim than he has been in years. Midair, he crossed the ball between his legs, and rose toward the hoop, dunking the ball with his right hand as various members of the Pacers' staff let out a collective scream.

But it was Haliburton who screamed the loudest, releasing more than a year of pent-up angst.

He had a running bet with Justin Tallard, one of Indiana's physical therapists, that if he completed the dunk, named an Eastbay, Haliburton could skip his post-practice workout.

It's a dunk Haliburton hadn't regularly made since he was a 20-year-old rookie.

Later, Haliburton posted a video of the dunk to his social media accounts, and the message to the rest of the league was obvious.

I'm back.

The dunk signified Haliburton's flashy arrival, but it was a quieter moment a month later that sent an even louder signal.

Before the start of the season, Pacers players held a minicamp in Los Angeles.

At one point during a scrimmage, Haliburton fell to the floor. A few months before, everyone in the gym would have gone hush, waiting for him to get back to his feet, similar to what happened that night in Oklahoma City.

But this time, nothing happened. He got up. The game continued.

"That," he said, "makes me feel normal again."

stories.headline: WNBA playoffs 2026: The Valkyries' wild path from expansion team to the Finals
stories.summary: Two years ago, the Valkyries didn't exist. Now they're competing for their first title -- here's how they did it.
stories.body:
As a general rule, expansion teams aren't really supposed to be very good right away. Sure, the initial player draft offers a chance to assess the league's potentially undervalued and overlooked players on the off chance of finding a hidden treasure, but from there, contention usually requires a lot of patience: A bunch of losing seasons provide the high draft picks to slowly accumulate talent, with a legitimate chance to contend finally waiting at the end of that long building process.

The Golden State Valkyries apparently missed that memo.

Barely two seasons into their existence, the Valkyries are headed to the WNBA Finals against the Atlanta Dream (Game 1 at 12:30 p.m. Saturday). To get there, they closed out the Las Vegas Aces on the road. This was a matchup that began as a huge mismatch in team pedigree -- the Aces had won three of the past four WNBA titles, while Golden State literally didn't exist two years ago -- if not talent. Instead, it became a changing of the guard, with the league's new contender sweeping aside one of its greatest dynasties.

Exactly how historic are the Valkyries as a recent expansion team? And how have they managed to go from an expansion draft to a Finals appearance in less than two years? Let's dive into five charts that explain Golden State's unprecedented rise.

Going into 2025, it was a bit of a mystery how the Valkyries would end up doing in their first WNBA season. Previously, expansion teams had posted an average winning percentage of .306 with a minus-8.4 net rating (we're not including 1997, the league's first season). If history was any indication, fans could expect Golden State to be one of the league's worst teams out of the gates.

But before Golden State, the league hadn't added a new team since the Atlanta Dream in 2008, meaning a backlog of great players was building up in competition for the same number of total roster spots in the W. (Witness the number of high draft picks who would be waived heading into each season.) Contrary to the historical record, this suggested the Valkyries would be tapping into a vast reservoir of available talent when building the first WNBA expansion squad in nearly two decades.

And that has largely proved to be true. The Valkyries ended up having the second-best first-year winning percentage (.523) of any WNBA club -- trailing only the 1998 Detroit Shock (.567) -- and the best expansion year by both net rating (plus-1.8) and Elo rating (1494). And all they've done since is continued that meteoric rise, to the point that they had the best regular season for a second-year team by all available measures of team quality, and in fact finished with the second-best record in the league -- and best net rating overall -- in 2026.

As a result of their dramatic rise from, well, not having a team at all in 2024 to the league's top net rating in 2026, the Valkyries' odds of winning the WNBA title also have risen dramatically. Going into the season, Golden State looked like a solid pick to return to the playoffs and possibly even win a series (last year's season ended with a 2-0 first-round sweep to the Minnesota Lynx). But contending for the championship seemed like a much taller order -- especially in a crowded field that contained the former champion Aces and Liberty, plus the improved Olivia Miles version of the Lynx, an Indiana Fever team featuring a healthy Caitlin Clark, and the overhauled Dream.

And for the first few months of the season, that seemed about right. The Valkyries were 13-7 through the end of June, one of the better records in the league but still clearly within a five-team logjam below Minnesota and Las Vegas. It seemed as if Golden State were destined to spend all year fighting for razor-thin seeding margins within that group. But since July 1, the Valkyries rattled off a league-best 19-5 record and saw their odds in statistical systems like Elo zoom past those of the presumed-favorite Lynx by the end of the regular season, when the latter hit a late slump. A 5-1 playoff start has only reinforced their status as a serious title threat, and now the early-season underdog Valkyries are statistical favorites to win it all.

If we had to pick a single calling card for the Valkyries' impressive championship bid, it has to be their defense. With a defensive rating of 100.6, they not only led all teams in suppressing opponents' per-possession scoring, but the gap between Golden State and No. 2 Atlanta at 104.5 (3.9 points per 100 possessions) was roughly the same as the gap between Atlanta and No. 7 New York at 108.7 -- or nearly the gap to league average itself, which was 109.1. The Valkyries' difference compared to that league figure (minus-8.5 points per 100) ranked as the sixth-best single-season WNBA defense ever relative to average.

The 2025 Valkyries landed on a number of top-tier defenders through the expansion draft, including Veronica Burton on the perimeter and Temi Fagbenle on the inside, helping Golden State rank fourth on defense right out of the gate under coach Natalie Nakase. But an even more refined version of the team's D came into shape in 2026, with names like Kiah Stokes -- whose block saved the Valkyries in Game 2 against Vegas -- and Gabby Williams joining Burton this season.

The Valkyries' defensive recipe blends a few components. They have one of the better rim protectors in the league in Stokes, which contributes to a league-low 47.8 effective FG% allowed, plus a couple of premier ball hawks in Burton and Williams, which forces opponents into mistakes -- they also ranked No. 2 in turnover rate forced. And opponents don't get many easy transition opportunities against Golden State because the Valkyries play at the league's slowest pace and hardly ever turn the ball over. Nakase was the lead assistant under Becky Hammon for the 2023 Aces when they had one of the best defenses in WNBA history -- and now she's using those lessons to try to dethrone her old team.

Obviously, a team doesn't post the league's best net rating and fight to within a game of the WNBA Finals without star performances, and the Valkyries absolutely got one of those this season from Burton.

The Northwestern alum was originally taken No. 7 by Dallas in the 2022 draft, but the Wings never really gave her much opportunity to earn an expanded role; she started 19 only total games in her first two seasons, averaging a paltry 14.5 minutes over that span before being waived before the 2024 season. After signing with Connecticut midseason, Burton continued to log backup minutes (12.7 MPG) despite improving her scoring efficiency with increased usage.

It wasn't until Burton, left unprotected in the expansion draft, landed with Golden State that she finally found a situation in which she could start -- and she has thrived in the role. Averaging 29.0 MPG as a Valkyrie, Burton has remained one of the league's top defensive guards while also taking a huge step forward as an offensive presence, which earned her Most Improved Player honors in 2025. But the advanced metrics in particular adore Burton for her two-way play; her ability to draw fouls while still taking plenty of 3s; her playmaking (she maintained a 34.5% assist rate with just an 11.9% turnover rate); and her massive on-court impact, which showed up at both ends of the court. Burton finished the season ranked second behind only the MVP A'ja Wilson in both LAKER wins added and win shares.

Burton had help. Led by Williams, who arrived from Seattle as a big-time impact player in her own right, six additional Valkyries beyond Burton had at least 2.5 LAKER wins added; no other team in the league had more than five players crack that barrier, much less if their top star is tossed out. Add in Nakase, the 2025 WNBA Coach of the Year, and the Valkyries are loaded with talent from top to bottom.

As much as we've been extolling the virtues of Burton's game, she hasn't been as effective as usual in the playoffs -- averaging just 9.5 PPG on 35.3% shooting from the field in six games. She has still made her trademark on-court impact; Golden State has a plus-12.4 net rating when she's in the game, 13.3 points per 100 better than when she sits. And in the clutch, she made multiple big shots when Golden State needed her. But her postseason LAKER rating of plus-2.7 points per 100 is markedly down from her mark of plus-7.5 in the regular season.

Luckily for the Valkyries, they've received big performances from some of the other names on the roster -- most notably Williams, who is averaging 22.7 PPG in the playoffs. Another player who has run with an opportunity in Golden State, Williams was always more of a defensive player than a scorer in her previous career stops, but her usage rate this season (29.0%) was a whopping 11.2 points higher than her previous career average, and she's pushing it even higher (to 32.1%) in the playoffs.

Of course, Williams does have a tendency to raise her game in the postseason (where her career scoring average of 14.5 PPG is markedly higher than her 9.3 regular-season figure), but this is taking things to a new level. And the other Valkyries to raise their output significantly in the playoffs are Tiffany Hayes and Cecilia Zandalasini, who both have produced massive LAKER ratings (Hayes is at plus-10.7!) in around 18 minutes per game off the bench.

It should be noted that the Valkyries' run has involved its fair share of gritty wins, surviving Dallas in a win-or-go-home Game 3 to win in the first round, needing some late free throws and a last-second block to take the 2-0 lead over Las Vegas, and then outlasting the Aces in overtime of the semifinals clincher. There's no question Golden State will have another tough assignment taking down Angel Reese and the Dream -- and the league's second-best defense -- to win a title.

But the Valkyries have spent their entire, brief existence defying conventional expectations for expansion teams. Why should the most significant step yet along their improbable path to a championship be any different?

stories.headline: Formula 1 to return to Africa in 'early 2030s' as Rwanda race confirmed
stories.summary: Formula 1 is set to return to the African continent for the first time since 1993 after the sport confirmed a ten-year deal to host a race in Rwanda from "the early 2030s."
stories.body:
Formula 1 is set to return to the African continent for the first time since 1993 after the sport confirmed a 10-year deal to host a race in Rwanda from "the early 2030s."

After years of speculation about a return to the continent, F1 announced its plans for the "African Grand Prix" in a statement with Rwanda's president Paul Kagame on Tuesday.

The precise starting date of the new contract was not specified and is reliant on the construction of a purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 40 kilometres south of Rwanda's capital Kigali, which is set to be completed "early in the next decade."

The track, which will be built adjacent to the new Kigali International Airport, will be developed to the FIA Grade 1 standards required for F1 racing.

The last F1 race on the continent took place in South Africa in 1993 on the Kyalami circuit near Johannesburg, and Kagame described the sport's arrival in Rwanda as a moment that "belongs to Africa."

"For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement," Kagame said.

"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.

"This ten-year partnership is also an investment in Rwanda's future. The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."

F1's statement said the new circuit would "will be designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans."

It confirmed the circuit would be used for other international motorsport events during the rest of the year.

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali, who has long held an ambition for the sport to return to F1, said: "Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1. With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the World Championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.

"Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact.

"I would like to thank His Excellency Paul Kagame, President of the Republic of Rwanda, the Government of Rwanda, the Rwanda Development Board, FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem and everyone whose dedication and collaboration have made this possible."

As recently as last weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton spoke of the importance of F1 returning to Africa in the coming years.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Rwanda F1 race: Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen welcome prospect

"I've always said that we need to have a Grand Prix in Africa," Hamilton said. "It is, for me, the most important continent and the most beautiful continent. We're on all the other continents but that one and there should be no reason for it.

"It's something I've been pushing for in the background and Stefano's been amazing -- he's flown to Africa so many times over the last couple of years speaking to lots of different people and so I hope he has some news for me soon."

The grand prix in Rwanda will be added to an already packed F1 calendar, which is currently maxed out with the sport's self-imposed limit of 24 rounds per season.

Races in Portugal and Türkiye's are set to return to the schedule next year, following on from the addition of a new venue in Madrid this year.

stories.headline: Ranking every AFL free agent by the impact they'll have at their new club
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL free agency period is now complete. We've ranked every move that has been made, factoring in positional needs and their likely impact for season 2027.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL free agency period is now complete, with seven players finding new clubs either as restricted or unrestricted free agents.

We've ranked every move that has been made, factoring in positional needs and their likely impact for season 2027 (not the rest of their career). So, who will be the biggest needle mover of the bunch in the immediate future?

7. Kieren Briggs
This is absolutely no criticism of Kieren Briggs, but there really aren't many players in the competition (if any) that could be dropped into the Tigers in 2027 and be serious needle movers. Remember, Richmond has won just 10 games across the last three seasons and is widely expected to finish in the bottom four once again next year. Tigers skipper Toby Nankervis will remain the club's primary ruck in the immediate future, but the arrival of Briggs will allow for a new-look one-two punch. The former Giant is one of the best hitout-to-advantage rucks in the game and an elite clearance winner. At 27 years of age, and with Nankervis now 32, Briggs' impact will likely be felt in the years beyond 2027.

6. Jordon Butts
Key defensive stocks have been a concern for the Bulldogs in recent years, so the signing of Jordon Butts will be a welcomed addition for the club. Butts makes the move after eight seasons and 94 games with the Crows, but he's managed just 10 and nine games in 2025 and 2026. Throughout different parts of the last couple of years, he's struggled with unlucky injuries; in 2025 it was a collapsed lung, and this year he battled concussion and a fractured foot. With the continued strong form of Josh Worrell and Mark Keane, and emergence of Josh Borlase at the Crows, a move to the Bulldogs makes sense for both the 26-year-old Butts and the Dogs.

5. Joel Amartey
The Blues landed key forward support for Harry McKay in the form of Joel Amartey, who crosses from the Swans as an unrestricted free agent. It's a shrewd acquisition for Carlton, and the club will be hopeful he can be an upgrade on both Brodie Kemp and Mitch McGovern. Amartey is coming off a season at Sydney in which he booted 28 goals from 15 games and averaged three marks per game. In 2024 he enjoyed a career-best 43-goal campaign, including a bag of nine against the Crows. Amartey is just 27 years of age and should only really be coming into his prime as a key position player in the AFL. Could surprise a few in 2027.

4. Toby Greene
Another year, another major coup for the Cats. Is anyone surprised?! Former Giants captain Toby Greene joins Geelong as an unrestricted free agent while GWS has to make do with second-round compensation. We all know Greene has been a high-impact player throughout his 15-year career and he will add a whole new dynamic to the Cats' forward line, one that features former Giants teammate and close friend Jeremy Cameron. In 2026, Greene kicked 34 goals -- his lowest return in a season since his injury-interrupted 2020 campaign -- but did amass over 20 disposals per game. If anyone wanted to argue he deserves the top spot on this list I wouldn't scoff, but it's not as if the Cats had trouble scoring in 2026...

3. Ben King
It may have been a move that surprised few, but it's one -- along with the signing of Zach Merrett, of course -- that will have Hawks fans believing a premiership is possible in 2027. For a fair chunk of the 2026 season, King looked to be the Coleman Medal winner. Gold Coast's capitulation didn't help his chances, though he still finished the home and away season with 60 goals to his name -- the third consecutive year he's managed 55+ goals. King will partner veteran Jack Gunston and dynamo Nick Watson in what now looks to be one of the most dangerous forward lines in the game.

2. Lachie Neale
The Lachie Neale-Brisbane Lions era is over, with the two-time Brownlow Medal winner joining Collingwood as an unrestricted free agent and partnering reigning Brownlow winner Nick Daicos in a new-look Magpies midfield. Neale might be 33 years of age and on the downturn of his decorated career, but he still averaged 29 disposals, 12.5 contested possessions, and six clearances per outing in 2026 and figures to be a major contributor next season in a Collingwood engine room that's often lacked depth and firepower. Even if the Magpies receive 80-85% of this season's production from Neale, he'll be difficult to top as the most impactful free agent of the year.

1. Zak Butters
The most sought after man in football made the decision to sign with the Bulldogs during free agency. Former Power star Zak Butters joins the club as a top five player in the game, and at age 26, you can certainly make the argument he's only at the beginning of his prime. Butters will partner Western Bulldogs skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards in what's easily the most impressive and dynamic three-pronged midfield in the competition. He offers a real point of difference, too, with his electric pace and the ability to break lines two eye-catching features that have seen him ascend to footy superstardom.

stories.headline: St. Louis unbeaten run up to 20 games, tying Red Bulls' MLS record
stories.summary: Carlo Holse's hat trick helped St. Louis City SC beat the LA Galaxy 6-2 on Sunday night to extend their unbeaten streak across all competitions to 20 games.
stories.body:
ST. LOUIS -- Carlo Holse's hat trick in the first 21 minutes -- the second hat trick in club history -- helped St. Louis City beat the LA Galaxy 6-2 on Sunday night to extend their unbeaten streak across all competitions to 20 games and tie the MLS record.

St. Louis, which is 13-0-5 in its last 18 regular-season games, tied the mark set when the New York Red Bulls went unbeaten in an MLS-record 20 consecutive games across all competitions in 2016.

Rafael Navarro converted from the penalty spot in the 45th minute, scored again in the 53rd and added two assists for St. Louis (14-6-8). Lukas MacNaughton scored on a diving header in the seventh minute of first-half stoppage time and Roman Bürki had five saves.

Holse opened the scoring in the second minute, added a goal in the seventh and skipped a shot inside the right post from the center of the area to make it 3-0 in the 21st minute to record the second-fastest hat trick in MLS history. Hany Mukhtar scored three goals for Nashville in the first 16 minutes of 5-1 win over Chicago on July 17, 2021.

The Galaxy's Kyōgo Furuhashi went off due to an apparent hamstring injury and was replaced in the 10th minute by João Klauss, whose goal in the 71st minute capped the scoring. Klauss, a 29-year-old midfielder in his first season with the Galaxy, had St. Louis City's first hat trick in a 3-3 tie with the Galaxy on June 14, 2025.

Robert Taylor scored in the 31st minute for the Galaxy (9-11-9).

St. Louis beat the Galaxy 3-1 on July 22 at Dignity Health Sports Park and hosts the Vancouver Whitecaps on Wednesday in a Western Conference top-of-table clash.

The Galaxy, who are clinging to the last playoff spot in the West, play the Portland Timbers at Dignity Health Sports Park on Wednesday. The Timbers are three points behind the Galaxy for ninth place -- the final playoff spot.

Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

stories.headline: New Zealand Rugby launches legal action against ARLC over 'Chiefs' name
stories.summary: The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.
stories.body:
The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.

NZR on Thursday said it had been left with no choice but to launch legal proceedings against the ARLC, who has sought to adopt the name for its Papua New Guinea expansion franchise.

The PNG Chiefs are due to join the NRL in 2028 and have already signed a raft of players, including code-hoppers Zac Lomaz and Joey Manu, but they may yet have to undergo a chanGe of name if NZR gets its way.

The Chiefs' Super Rugby franchise has existed since 1996, with NZR claiming the introduction of the PNG Chiefs would result in "significant confusion and damage" should they be allowed to compete under the name from 2028.

"New Zealand Rugby (NZR) has today moved to protect the Chiefs brand and is filing proceedings in the High Court of New Zealand against the decision by the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) to launch a new NRL side using "Chiefs" in its name," an NZR statement read.  

"NZR is seeking both an interim and final injunction which stops the use of the names 'PNG Chiefs', 'Chiefs' or any other similar names in New Zealand.   

"The Chiefs have competed as a professional rugby team in Super Rugby since 1996 and over those 30 years, have built a strong identity and fanbase across New Zealand, Australia and internationally.  

"In New Zealand, NZR owns both the trademark rights for the word Chiefs and the Chiefs logo and since 1998, NZR has also held trademark protection for the Chiefs logo in Australia."

NZR claims it had tried to engage with the ARLC in an attempt to find a resolution, yet the commission was now intent on proceeding with the official launch of the PNG Chiefs on Oct. 21.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said. "We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand.   

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific. We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."  

The Chiefs won two Super Rugby titles in back-to-back seasons in 2012 and 2013, and were runners-up in Super Rugby Pacific this season after suffering a crushing defeat by the Hurricanes in the decider.

The Hamilton-based team has produced countless All Blacks since its inception, with Saturday's run-on team to face the Wallabies featuring six players from the franchise.

"Here in New Zealand, when people hear 'the Chiefs', they think of this club and this region. The identity carries significant cultural meaning and connection to the region and its people, we know it means a great deal to our players and coaches past and present, fans and supporters here and around the world," Chiefs CEO Simon Graafhuis said.   

"Teams in different sports and markets can exist alongside one another with the same name, but the issue here is the similarity of our sports competing in the same market, for the same fans, in overlapping windows."  

However, ARLC executive chairman Peter V'Landys later issued a stinging rebuke, insisting he would vigorously defend PNG's right to use the Chiefs as its team name.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval. The NSW Blues had been the Blues for in excess of 50 years before that," he said.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

No date has yet been slated for the hearing in New Zealand's High Court.
